paragraphs: Bilevel optimization describes learning problems with two linked minimization tasks: decisions at one level depend on decisions at the other. This structure appears in reinforcement learning and meta-learning. When tasks run on different computing resources, solving the coupled problem also requires coordinating the participating agents.

The paper introduces SLAM, a stochastic linearized augmented Lagrangian method for nonconvex bilevel optimization over a communication graph. Its coordination mechanism allows agents to reach agreement on variables at both optimization levels. This matters because agreement on only one set of variables would leave part of the coupled learning problem unresolved.

The theoretical result concerns convergence to Karush-Kuhn-Tucker points, which satisfy constrained optimization conditions rather than necessarily being global minima. SLAM achieves a convergence rate of the same order as classical distributed stochastic gradient descent for single-level nonconvex problems. Numerical experiments on multi-agent reinforcement learning also show advantages over the tested benchmarks. Together, these results support decentralized bilevel learning without a worse convergence-rate order than the stated single-level comparison.
neurips-2022-a-stochastic-linearized-aug.tldr: SLAM coordinates decentralized bilevel learning and achieves convergence to KKT points at the same rate order as distributed single-level stochastic gradient descent.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves producing outputs whose parts are related, making their agreement useful information for a model. Conditional random fields provide a way to represent such relationships, but their computational cost and practical performance have often made standalone deep networks more attractive. Earlier combinations of the two have also struggled to match strong neural approaches.

This paper proposes a generic combination in which a log-supermodular conditional random field serves as a regularizer for a deep network. Its role is to encourage similarity between outputs within the structured prediction task. The approach therefore adds an explicit preference for coordinated predictions to the underlying neural solution.

The authors report that this combination applies broadly and adds only moderate computational overhead to the base network. In some cases, it can match carefully engineered approaches built entirely from deep networks. That qualification is central: the finding supports a practical way to improve generic frameworks, rather than establishing that adding this regularizer always beats specialized architectures. Its contribution is making structured output relationships useful at a manageable additional cost.
neurips-2022-boosting-the-performance-of.tldr: A log-supermodular CRF regularizer encourages coordinated neural predictions with moderate overhead and can rival specialized deep networks in some cases.

paragraphs: The paper studies convex objectives that split into many component functions, each depending on only some coordinates of the shared parameter vector. The functions are Lipschitz but need not be smooth. A common strategy samples one component at a time, yet the effectiveness of that approach relies on how uniformly the components behave, as captured by a condition number.

The proposed algorithm instead chooses components adaptively through a combination of cutting-plane and interior-point methods. Its gradient-computation bound depends on the sum of the numbers of coordinates used by the individual components. This makes the decomposed structure directly relevant to the theoretical cost of optimization.

Up to suppressed logarithmic factors, the bound is the sum of those coordinate counts multiplied by log(1/epsilon), with no condition-number assumption. The previous condition-number-independent cutting-plane bound uses the number of components times the full parameter dimension, also multiplied by log(1/epsilon). The improvement can therefore exploit components with small coordinate supports. The authors also derive an improved evaluation-oracle bound for decomposable submodular minimization.
neurips-2022-decomposable-non-smooth-con.tldr: An adaptive optimization method exploits component coordinate supports to reduce gradient-oracle complexity without assumptions on the condition number.

paragraphs: Ranked preferences tell a decision maker which alternatives an agent prefers, but not how much more valuable one alternative is than another. That missing information can make an allocation poor in terms of total social welfare. Distortion measures the performance loss caused by making decisions with this limited preference information.

The paper studies whether a small amount of additional information can improve matching and related allocation decisions. It considers mechanisms that supplement rankings with queries about actual values. The covered problem class includes one-sided matching, two-sided matching, general graph matching, and resource allocation with a constraint on the number of selected resources.

The authors design two-query mechanisms with the best possible worst-case distortion for the setting studied. Their guarantees also improve on the best possible expected distortion of randomized mechanisms that use rankings alone. This comparison shows that limited value elicitation can provide a stronger welfare guarantee than randomization over ordinal information. The result concerns how well mechanisms perform under their information restrictions, rather than a claim that two queries recover every agent's full preferences.
neurips-2022-don-t-roll-the-dice-ask-twi.tldr: For a broad matching and allocation class, two-query mechanisms achieve optimal worst-case distortion and outperform the best expected distortion from randomized ranking-only mechanisms.

paragraphs: Multi-label image recognition asks a model to identify several categories that may appear in the same image. Learning this with few annotations is difficult because the available labels provide limited supervision. DualCoOp addresses the problem by using an existing vision-language model whose image and text representations were aligned through millions of auxiliary image-text pairs.

Its main mechanism is dual context optimization: learnable linguistic contexts describe both positive and negative cases alongside class names. These prompts adapt the pretrained model to deciding whether categories are present. The framework adds only a small learnable component, allowing it to draw on the existing alignment without requiring a large new annotation-dependent model.

The same framework supports recognition with partial labels and recognition involving unseen classes. Experiments on standard benchmarks in these two low-label settings show advantages over the compared state-of-the-art methods. The stated findings support lightweight prompt adaptation as a way to use broad image-text pretraining for multi-label decisions. They also connect fast adaptation to the small amount of additional learned machinery.
neurips-2022-dualcoop-fast-adaptation-to.tldr: DualCoOp learns lightweight positive and negative prompts to adapt pretrained vision-language models to multi-label recognition with partial labels or unseen classes.

paragraphs: An optimizer determines how a learning system updates its parameters from gradient information. This paper treats the design of that update rule as a search problem that can run directly on the task of interest. The motivation is to make optimizer discovery more scalable and efficient than approaches limited by costly searches or weak transfer across tasks.

The key representation starts from a simple observation: update rules are mathematical expressions with a tree structure. The authors organize candidate optimizers into a larger tree in which each path encodes a rule. Searching for an optimizer then becomes a path-finding problem, opening the process to established tree-search techniques.

Their algorithm adapts Monte Carlo tree search and adds rejection sampling and detection of equivalent expressions to improve sample efficiency. On a diverse collection of benchmark tasks, the framework discovers optimizers that outperform both human-designed alternatives and earlier optimizer-search methods using 128 evaluations. The findings show that this representation can make useful optimizer discovery possible with a limited evaluation budget on the tested tasks.
neurips-2022-efficient-non-parametric-op.tldr: Representing optimizer formulas as paths through a tree enables efficient searches that discover strong task-specific update rules in 128 evaluations.

paragraphs: A robot learning over time must recognize new objects while retaining what it learned before. It may receive unlabeled data from either a new task or a previously encountered one, with only a small budget for asking a person to supply labels. The paper formalizes this combination as Few-Shot Continual Active Learning.

The framework represents each object category with a uniform Gaussian mixture model. It uses pseudo-rehearsal to reduce catastrophic forgetting, the loss of earlier knowledge during subsequent learning. It also measures uncertainty using the Gaussian representations of previously learned categories and uses that information to select samples for labeling. These components address retention and label selection within the same learning process.

Evaluation covers the CORe-50 object dataset and an actual humanoid robot. The authors report state-of-the-art dataset results and demonstrate that the robot can learn previously unseen objects in a real environment with limited user labeling. The results support combining continual learning with active sample selection when an agent must keep learning without receiving extensive annotations at every increment.
neurips-2022-few-shot-continual-active-l.tldr: A framework combining Gaussian class representations, pseudo-rehearsal, and uncertainty-based label selection enables continual object learning with limited supervision.

paragraphs: Graph embedding maps nodes into representations intended to preserve useful relationships. Contrastive methods encourage similar nodes to stay close and dissimilar nodes to separate. The paper revisits this objective through two scatter matrices: one captures graph connectivity, while the other incorporates the spread associated with negative sampling.

The proposed GLEN framework uses a rank-difference objective to seek a representation with a minimum class-separation guarantee. Direct rank-based optimization is computationally difficult, so the authors replace it with a difference of log-determinant expressions. They argue that this is a more accurate approximation to the rank objective than the trace difference used by the earlier COLES framework.

The analysis also connects the log-determinant difference to established geometric measures between matrices, providing lower and upper bounds involving those measures. These relationships give mathematical structure to the proposed surrogate rather than treating it solely as a convenient numerical replacement. Empirically, GLEN offers favorable accuracy and scalability compared with the tested state-of-the-art baselines, supporting the practical value of reconsidering the objective used to separate graph representations.
neurips-2022-generalized-laplacian-eigen.tldr: GLEN uses a log-determinant surrogate for a rank-based graph embedding objective and reports favorable accuracy and scalability.

paragraphs: Safe exploration requires learning about an unknown constraint without evaluating parameter choices that violate it. A Gaussian process can represent uncertainty about that constraint and identify regions believed safe with high probability. The challenge is deciding which safe evaluation will teach the learner the most.

The paper proposes an information-theoretic selection criterion that uses the Gaussian process posterior directly. It chooses informative parameters from the safe region, linking the exploration decision to the current uncertainty about the constraint. Unlike approaches built around a discretized domain, the method naturally applies to continuous parameter spaces and introduces no additional hyperparameters of the kind discussed in the abstract.

The theoretical analysis establishes high-probability safety and learning of the constraint to arbitrary precision. The safety statement remains probabilistic: it does not assert unconditional freedom from violations. Empirical evaluations also show improved data efficiency and scalability. Together, the results support directing safe evaluations toward information gain while avoiding the extra discretization and tuning requirements identified in the motivating methods.
neurips-2022-information-theoretic-safe-.tldr: An information-theoretic Gaussian-process criterion selects informative safe evaluations in continuous domains, with high-probability safety guarantees.

paragraphs: Knowledge base completion fills missing relationships between entities. This paper proposes doing so through prototype entities: to infer an entity's missing relationship, find another entity that shares the relevant relationship. The prototype supplies an interpretable intermediate connection, making the prediction explainable through a concrete instance.

The authors develop theory for modeling these prototypes and for combining instance-based learning with translational models. Experiments across several tasks support the resulting model's effectiveness and interpretability. The contribution therefore includes both a prediction method and a way to express why a particular entity is useful evidence for a missing fact.

The paper also reexamines how rule-based completion methods work. Some rules, it argues, express instance-based equivalence rather than a semantically compatible link between premise and conclusion. Although these instance-based rules occupy only a small part of the rule space, they outperform the remaining rules on all four studied benchmarks. Additional experiments support their role in rule-based models' effectiveness, suggesting that interpreting rules requires attention to the prototype relationships they encode.
neurips-2022-instance-based-learning-for.tldr: Prototype-based reasoning improves interpretable knowledge base completion and offers evidence that instance equivalence helps explain the success of rule-based models.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories to individual image pixels or points in a three-dimensional scene. Dense labels for this task are costly, so weakly supervised methods learn from less detailed annotations. This paper uses classification labels alone while jointly learning from images and point clouds, allowing the two domains to help each other.

Information moves in both directions. Image class activation maps indicate regions associated with a category, and projection turns these maps into self-supervision for the point-cloud model. In the reverse direction, similarities among point-cloud features help train the image classifier toward more precise segmentation. Confidence-based scores reduce the influence of inaccurate self-generated supervision in both transfers.

The experiments report improvements in both image and point-cloud segmentation, with substantial gains over prior weakly supervised approaches on ScanNetV2. Quantitative and qualitative results support the claim that useful information transfers in both directions. The approach matters because it treats available two-dimensional and three-dimensional observations as complementary training signals, rather than learning each segmentation problem independently from the same limited level of human annotation.
neurips-2022-joint-learning-of-2d-3d-wea.tldr: A joint framework lets images and point clouds supervise each other, improving both forms of semantic segmentation using classification labels alone.

paragraphs: Stochastic shortest path problems describe goal-directed decisions with uncertain outcomes. Solving them can become computationally difficult even at moderate sizes. The paper targets a further challenge: reusing planning knowledge across related problems whose objects have different names or whose object counts differ.

The proposed Generalized Policy Automata are nondeterministic partial policies that help accelerate the solution process. They are learned through relational, feature-based abstractions, so the learned guidance is expressed through reusable properties and relationships. Because the policies are partial, their role is to assist planning across a problem family rather than prescribe every decision in every possible state.

The theoretical analysis establishes completeness and hierarchical optimality for the approach. Hierarchical optimality is the stated guarantee, and should not be read as an unrestricted claim of global optimality. Empirically, the method learns broadly applicable policy knowledge from few examples and substantially outperforms the compared solvers on test instances with many more objects than the training instances. This supports abstraction as a way to carry useful planning structure into larger problems.
neurips-2022-learning-generalized-policy.tldr: Relational policy automata learn reusable partial planning guidance that transfers to larger stochastic shortest path problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find a low-dimensional subspace that minimizes a smooth convex loss. This covers extensions of principal component analysis, including robust, sparse, and binary-data variants. Although the loss is convex, the subspace search is nonconvex, creating a trade-off between inexpensive iterations and straightforward guarantees about reaching a global solution.

The authors connect nonconvex methods with a convex relaxation under a strict complementarity assumption. In this setting, the relaxation has a unique optimum that also solves the original problem. That connection lets the analysis use the convex formulation to justify fast behavior of methods operating directly on the subspace.

The main result proves local linear convergence for a gradient method that avoids singular value decomposition and needs one QR factorization of an n-by-k matrix per iteration. Local linear convergence means geometric error reduction when starting sufficiently near the solution; it is not an arbitrary-initialization guarantee. The paper also establishes linear convergence results for nonconvex projected gradient and for Frank-Wolfe applied to the relaxation.
neurips-2022-local-linear-convergence-of.tldr: Under strict complementarity, an SVD-free subspace gradient method has provably local linear convergence with one small QR factorization per iteration.

paragraphs: Video action recognition often uses only a few frames because processing many frames is expensive. That shortcut can discard useful evidence about the action. The proposed Ample and Focal Network addresses this tension by dividing the work between a branch that gathers broad information and a branch that concentrates computation on salient frames.

The Ample Branch processes all input frames with condensed computation. A Navigation Module uses its information to guide the Focal Branch, which reduces the temporal size at each convolution block. The two branches' outputs are then adaptively combined to retain information from both broad coverage and selective processing.

The authors show that this design can process more frames with less computation. They also report that it can achieve higher accuracy with fewer frames, attributing this to dynamic selection of intermediate features that implicitly models temporal relationships. An extension reduces spatial redundancy as well. Experiments across five datasets support the method's efficiency and effectiveness, showing how selection within the network can improve the balance between video coverage and computational cost.
neurips-2022-look-more-but-care-less-in-.tldr: AFNet combines inexpensive broad frame processing with dynamically focused computation to improve video recognition efficiency and accuracy.

paragraphs: A visual reinforcement learning policy may perform well in its training environment yet fail when backgrounds or image statistics change. The paper connects this weakness to which pixels influence the policy's decisions. Its central idea is that a policy should consistently identify useful visual evidence and avoid relying on irrelevant parts of the image.

Saliency-guided Q-networks turn that intuition into a training method for visual reinforcement learning. Saliency identifies image regions important to a decision, providing guidance about where learning should focus. The method aims to preserve this identification across images and is described as compatible with any approach that learns a value function.

Experiments using Soft Actor-Critic agents report large improvements in generalization. On the DeepMind Control Generalization benchmark, SGQN outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods, with reported benefits in training efficiency, the gap between training and generalization performance, and policy interpretability. The findings support using decision-relevant visual information as a training signal for policies that must cope with distracting or altered observations.
neurips-2022-look-where-you-look-salienc.tldr: Saliency-guided Q-networks improve visual control generalization by training policies to focus consistently on pixels relevant to their decisions.

paragraphs: OGC learns to separate multiple objects in three-dimensional point clouds without human annotations. Its source of supervision is the motion visible across successive point clouds. The central idea is that rigid motion and consistent object shape provide evidence about which points belong to the same object.

The system combines three components: an object segmentation network, an auxiliary self-supervised scene-flow estimator, and an object geometry consistency component. Scene flow supplies motion information, while the consistency component connects that information to object structure. The training losses account for multiple objects' rigid behavior and shape invariance across both space and time.

Although learning uses sequential motion patterns, the segmentation network predicts multiple object masks from a single point-cloud frame in one forward pass. This distinction explains how temporal evidence can train a model whose segmentation input is a single frame. Evaluations on five datasets report strong performance for object-part instance segmentation and general object segmentation, including indoor and challenging outdoor settings. The results support rigid dynamics as a useful source of annotation-free object supervision.
neurips-2022-ogc-unsupervised-3d-object-.tldr: OGC uses rigid motion and geometry consistency across point-cloud sequences to learn single-frame multi-object segmentation without human labels.

paragraphs: The paper studies an attacker who can replace an eta fraction of training examples to make a learner fail on a particular test point. The attacker knows that target, while the learner does not. The question is how small the learner's error can be despite this targeted poisoning.

In the realizable setting, where the hypothesis class can represent the correct labeling, the optimal error scales as VC dimension times eta, up to constant factors. A deterministic learner can attain the upper bound. In the agnostic setting, the authors obtain error bounded by a constant greater than one times the best achievable class error, plus a poisoning term proportional to VC dimension times eta.

The agnostic analysis also shows that every deterministic learner faces an attack forcing error to at least twice the best class error. Thus, multiplicative deterioration is unavoidable there. The optimal-rate algorithms may output hypotheses outside the original class. For several natural classes, including linear classifiers, proper learners retain linear dependence on eta in the realizable setting, with a polynomial dependence on VC dimension hidden in the constants.
neurips-2022-on-optimal-learning-under-t.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal realizable learning error under targeted poisoning and proves an unavoidable multiplicative penalty for deterministic agnostic learners.

paragraphs: A receiver operating characteristic curve describes trade-offs between true positive and false positive rates in binary classification. This paper asks which curve an estimation procedure should target when its available model family may be misspecified. It defines an optimal ROC curve relative to a general model space, making the available models part of the target itself.

The authors analyze three popular estimation methods at the population level, where sampling uncertainty is removed by considering infinitely many observations. When the model space contains all measurable classifiers and the surrogate loss meets specified conditions, all three methods are consistent. Some of those loss conditions resemble conditions used to guarantee classification consistency.

Misspecification changes the conclusion: only one of the three analyzed methods consistently estimates the optimal ROC curve within the chosen model space. Numerical results illustrate how model restrictions affect the resulting estimates. The finding matters because consistency in a sufficiently rich model family does not automatically carry over to a restricted one, even when the target is defined relative to that restriction.
neurips-2022-on-the-consistent-estimatio.tldr: Among three analyzed ROC estimators, only one remains consistent for the chosen model space under model misspecification.

paragraphs: The paper empirically examines how pre-training Transformers on language or image data affects their subsequent fine-tuning on MuJoCo offline reinforcement learning tasks. Its focus is on understanding what these earlier learning experiences contribute when the models are adapted to a different kind of task.

The researchers inspect internal representations and parameter changes. Pre-training substantially changes the models’ representations, yet during fine-tuning the pre-trained models acquire less information from the task data than a randomly initialized model. Their parameters also change relatively little. For the image-pre-trained model, the analysis suggests that large gradients and gradient clipping could partly explain poor performance. This identifies a possible contributing mechanism, rather than establishing a complete explanation.

To investigate what language pre-training contributes, the researchers fine-tune the language-pre-trained model without providing context. It still learns efficiently in this setting. Follow-up analysis supports the hypothesis that language pre-training gives the Transformer access to something resembling contextual information that it can use on the downstream task. The finding suggests that the benefit may involve information acquired during pre-training, even when context is absent during fine-tuning.
neurips-2022-on-the-effect-of-pre-traini.tldr: Language-pre-trained Transformers learn efficiently without supplied context in the studied offline reinforcement learning setting, supporting a hypothesis that pre-training provides context-like information.

paragraphs: The Santa Claus problem allocates items among agents to maximize the value received by the least well-served agent. Both the items and the agents' valuations can differ. This paper studies the online version, in which each item must be assigned when it arrives, before the remaining items are known.

An arbitrary arrival order prevents a good worst-case guarantee. With a random arrival order, however, the authors obtain a competitive ratio of 1 minus epsilon under a size condition on the optimal allocation. Assuming each item has value at most one, every agent's value in that optimal allocation must be at least on the order of log(n) divided by epsilon squared.

The paper also proves a lower bound: when the optimal minimum value is at most C times ln(n) divided by epsilon for a constant C, no algorithm can achieve that competitive ratio, even with random ordering. The bounds are described as almost tight. Together, they show that random arrival helps, but near-optimal online fairness still depends on sufficiently large attainable value per agent.
neurips-2022-online-algorithms-for-the-s.tldr: Random item order enables nearly optimal online fair allocation when every agent's optimal value is sufficiently large, with an almost matching impossibility bound.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks are useful models of local neural activity, but studying several interacting brain areas calls for theory about connected networks. Stability of each individual component does not by itself answer when the whole assembly will remain stable. This paper takes a constructive approach to identifying combinations that preserve stability.

The authors use nonlinear control theory and machine learning to derive conditions for assembling stable RNNs. These conditions allow extensive feedback connections between the component networks, making them relevant to systems with substantial interaction. They also parameterize the conditions so that the resulting assemblies can be optimized with gradient-based training.

Experiments show that networks trained under these stability constraints can perform well on challenging sequential-processing benchmarks. This supports the compatibility of the proposed stability structure with useful sequence computation, rather than treating stability as an analysis applied only after training. The broader contribution is a principled construction for studying distributed, modular neural computation through interacting recurrent components, while keeping the stability guarantee tied to the derived conditions.
neurips-2022-rnns-of-rnns-recursive-cons.tldr: Trainable conditions allow stable recurrent networks to be assembled into larger stable systems with extensive feedback connections.

paragraphs: Restoring a degraded face is ambiguous because the input may no longer contain enough detail to determine a clear output. CodeFormer addresses this by learning a discrete codebook of visual building blocks in a compact representation space. Restoration becomes a task of predicting codes, which reduces uncertainty in the mapping and supplies detail for generating a high-quality face.

A Transformer predicts these codes using the face's global composition and context. This allows the system to combine information across the degraded image when choosing a plausible reconstruction. The paper also introduces a controllable feature transformation module that adjusts the balance between fidelity to the target and visual quality for different degradation conditions.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report better quality and fidelity than the compared state-of-the-art methods, along with stronger robustness to degradation. The stated results include severely degraded inputs, where CodeFormer can produce natural faces closely approximating the targets. Its contribution is combining a constrained set of learned visual elements with global prediction and an adjustable restoration trade-off.
neurips-2022-towards-robust-blind-face-r.tldr: CodeFormer restores degraded faces by predicting learned visual codes with a Transformer and provides control over the fidelity–quality trade-off.

paragraphs: Collaborative machine learning lets parties pool their datasets to obtain better models than they could train individually. Rewarding participation involves both access to model performance and the allocation of payoffs. This paper studies how to balance those rewards fairly, including situations where participants face different budget constraints.

The initial allocation scheme assumes parties can afford the optimal model trained on all the combined data. The authors derive the same scheme in two ways: from desirable properties of the parties' final payoffs, and from desirable properties of the payoff flows between parties. Agreement between these derivations connects fairness of the outcome with fairness of the transfers producing it.

The flow-based view also provides a way to address limited budgets. The authors specify properties for fairly adjusting transfers while trading model performance against payoff rewards. Empirical studies across collaborative learning scenarios with different budgets indicate that the scheme behaves sensibly. The contribution is therefore a framework for adapting the reward arrangement to affordability constraints, with its initial allocation result explicitly tied to the stated affordability assumption.
neurips-2022-trade-off-between-payoff-an.tldr: A collaborative learning allocation scheme connects fair payoffs with fair transfer flows and supports budget-dependent trade-offs between model performance and payoff rewards.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks communicate through discrete spikes over time, making them attractive for biological modeling and low-power neuromorphic computing. Their binary firing behavior also complicates training. Learning through spike timing can operate in an event-driven fashion with lower computation and memory use, but prior timing-based methods have lagged behind recurrent-network-like training in accuracy.

The paper analyzes temporal backpropagation and proves a conservation property: the sum of gradients remains unchanged between fully connected and convolutional layers. Max pooling respects this property, while average pooling does not and can suffer vanishing gradients. The authors show that average pooling can be revised to meet the requirement.

They also identify a reverse-gradient problem in timing-based learning and propose a backward kernel that resolves it while preserving the gradient-sum property. Experiments achieve state-of-the-art CIFAR10 results among time-based training methods. The authors additionally report the first successful training of an SNN on CIFAR100 using time-based backpropagation. These results connect analysis of gradient behavior to improved capability within event-driven training.
neurips-2022-training-spiking-neural-net.tldr: Analyzing and correcting timing-gradient behavior improves event-driven spiking-network training, including leading reported CIFAR10 performance among time-based methods.

paragraphs: In-context learning means using examples in a prompt to answer a new query without updating model parameters. This paper investigates that ability in controlled function classes. It asks whether training a Transformer on examples from some functions can teach it to infer other, unseen functions from the same class at inference time.

The experiments show that standard Transformers trained from scratch can learn unseen linear functions from prompt examples with performance comparable to an optimal least-squares estimator. The authors also demonstrate in-context learning under two forms of distribution shift: changes between training data and inference prompts, and differences between the prompt examples and the query input. These are empirical demonstrations in the studied settings.

The investigation extends to sparse linear functions and two-layer neural networks. For sparse functions, the Transformer beats least squares and nearly matches Lasso. For two-layer networks, it performs comparably to networks trained on the prompt examples using gradient descent. The findings show that in-context adaptation can reproduce useful function-learning behavior across several classes without inference-time parameter updates.
neurips-2022-what-can-transformers-learn.tldr: Transformers trained on function families empirically learn unseen functions from prompt examples, matching strong estimators in several studied settings without parameter updates.
